heading: Cradle of empires and faiths
body: Bihar's claim on Indian history is disproportionate to its present-day profile: for close to a thousand years, the region now called Bihar was where empires were run from and where two of the world's major religions took shape. Gautama Buddha is held to have attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, under a descendant of the original bodhi tree, making the site the spiritual center of Buddhism worldwide; the Mahabodhi Temple built there, substantially in its present form by the 5th–6th century CE, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the few structures from that era still standing in continuous use. A few decades earlier, Vaishali — also in Bihar — was the birthplace of Mahavira, the last Tirthankara of Jainism, and later hosted the second Buddhist council.

Politically, Bihar was the seat of power for the subcontinent's first great empire. Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire around 322 BCE from the capital Pataliputra (modern Patna), and his grandson Ashoka ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from the same city — until the Kalinga War, after which Ashoka renounced further conquest and became Buddhism's most consequential royal patron, sending missions as far as Sri Lanka and the Hellenistic Mediterranean. Centuries later the Gupta Empire, often described as a golden age of Indian science, mathematics and literature, likewise had its roots in the same region.

That intellectual legacy produced Nalanda, founded under Gupta patronage in the 5th century CE and sustained by later dynasties into the 12th century — a residential monastic university that drew scholars from China, Korea, Tibet and Southeast Asia, and that historians and UNESCO both describe as among the world's earliest institutions of higher learning. Its ruins, and the Mahabodhi Temple, are the anchor points for Bihar's entries on the map; both are places where a claim to "oldest" or "first" is unusually well documented rather than folklore.

The dates above (Nalanda's precise founding year, and the exact chronology of Ashoka's conversion relative to the Kalinga War) are debated among historians in their particulars, though not in the broad outline given here.
